analysis.one_liner: Ends fracking's exemption from Safe Drinking Water Act rules and requires disclosure of fracking chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate committee it was sent to, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close the 2005 loophole that exempts hydraulic fracturing from the Safe Drinking Water Act's rules on injecting fluids underground, letting the EPA regulate fracking wells like other injection wells. It would also require drilling companies to tell states what chemicals and sand mixtures they plan to pump into each well before drilling starts and what they actually used afterward, post that information on a public searchable website, and hand over trade-secret chemical identities to doctors and first responders during medical emergencies. It died in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking operations, especially those whose drinking water comes from wells or aquifers above the shale plays, would gain the right to know what chemicals are being injected thousands of feet below them and would be covered by federal underground-injection safeguards. Emergency responders and doctors would gain immediate access to proprietary chemical formulas when treating someone exposed to fracking fluids, without first needing paperwork the drilling company demanded.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near fracking sites and first responders

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds fracking to the definition of 'underground injection' under the Safe Drinking Water Act, repealing the 2005 exemption that kept fracking wells outside federal underground injection permitting [S2][S3].

It requires operators to disclose, before fracking starts and after it ends, the chemical constituents, CAS numbers, and amounts of every chemical and proppant injected, and requires states or EPA to verify the information and post it on a single public searchable website [S2][S3].
It lets states take over enforcement for fracking wells alone, so states could regulate without taking on the full federal underground injection program [S2][S3].

In a medical emergency, drillers must immediately disclose proprietary or trade-secret chemical formulas to the state, EPA, a first responder, or a health care provider, regardless of any confidentiality agreement, so exposure victims can be diagnosed and treated [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas drilling companies would bear the cost of complying with federal underground injection rules and of reporting chemical recipes for every well. Some operators argue these requirements add expense and slow drilling, costs that could be passed on through energy prices and reduced drilling activity in shale regions.

drawbacks.text: Operators would face new federal permitting and reporting requirements on every well, adding compliance costs to a drilling business that operates on thin margins at many wells, and opponents argue states already regulate fracking effectively [S2][S3].

Public posting of chemical lists, while protecting trade-secret formulas from public disclosure, would still reveal which chemicals a competitor uses at a site, information operators treat as commercially sensitive [S2][S3].

Health care workers and first responders who receive trade-secret formulas could share them for medical purposes but are barred from making them public, so the public website would not include the most closely held formulas [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is informational and preventive: people living above fracking operations would know what is being injected, and doctors would not be blocked by confidentiality agreements when treating an exposure. The main cost falls on drillers in the form of reporting and permitting compliance, and the bill's federal oversight would overlap with state programs in some states. On balance the public-health and disclosure gains are broad and the compliance costs are real but conventional regulatory burdens.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup, and died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Casey of Pennsylvania introduced the FRAC Act on June 11, 2013, with Senators Schumer, Gillibrand, Whitehouse, and Merkley as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S5].
Twelve senators—11 Democrats and 1 Independent—cosponsored the bill, but no further action was ever taken [S4][S5].
The committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill received no vote in either chamber before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas drilling companies are better off because the bill died: fracking remains exempt from Safe Drinking Water Act underground injection rules, and there is still no federal requirement to publicly disclose the chemicals used in each frack. The panel that oversees oil and gas fracking remained industry itself rather than the EPA or the public.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas drillers kept their exemption

for.name: Sen. Robert P. Casey, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FRAC Act to repeal fracking's exemption from the Safe Drinking Water Act and require chemical disclosure.

for.name: Sens. Chuck Schumer, Kirsten Gillibrand, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Joined Casey in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

against.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it received no committee action after referral and died at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal regulation of fracking and chemical disclosure requirements, and backed keeping the 2005 Safe Drinking Water Act exemption in place.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent who caucused with them, and no Republican signed on; there were no roll-call votes, so the partisan split is visible only in sponsorship.

industries.industry: Oil and gas drilling companies (hydraulic fracturing operators)
industries.note: The bill would end their exemption from federal underground injection rules and require chemical-by-chemical reporting for every well, including before-and-after disclosure and emergency access to trade-secret formulas. That information is exactly what nearby residents and emergency responders lack today.

Suppliers would face added documentation and their customers' formulas would be reported to regulators, though proprietary formulas would be shielded from public posting and emergency medical disclosure could stay confidential afterward.
